what: The ONE rule for 'does this head's type-I error block a release', written once and asserted by both implementations.
why: The rule exists twice because it must: the trainer decides `releaseEligible` in Python at train time,
and `releasability.mjs` decides the release in JavaScript at promote time. Neither language can import
the other, so CLAUDE.md's first two remedies for a fact stated twice -- delete a copy, derive one from
the other -- are both unavailable. That leaves the third: pin them equal with a test.
They HAD drifted, and it cost a diagnosis on 2026-08-25. The trainer blocked on `if falsePositive or
falseNegative`, a zero-tolerance rule left over from before Neyman-Pearson calibration. The gate had
moved on: bounded false positives are the POINT of an NP threshold, and `releasability.test.ts`
explicitly pins that false negatives must never block -- 'that bar is unclearable and was never the
point'. Both test suites passed. The contradiction lived between them, where no compiler could see it.
The candidate that exposed it was declared ineligible by SIX criteria. Five were inside the guarantee
they had been calibrated to. Retraining to satisfy them would have been tuning against a rule that
should not exist, while the one genuine failure stayed buried among the five.
axis: SUBTYPE, never criterion. The guarantee is computed per subtype, so that is the only level at which `permittedFalsePositives` means anything. The trainer used to aggregate to the criterion and compare against no bound at all, which is a second drift on top of the first.

cases.name: a clean head with a guarantee does not block
false positives INSIDE the bound do not block
cases.why: an NP threshold PERMITS bounded type-I error; that is what the bound is for. Observed on 1.3.1.

cases.name: false positives EXACTLY at the bound do not block
cases.why: the rank was chosen so that exactly this many negatives sit above the cut. Observed on 2.4.4, 2.4.6, 3.3.1 and 4.1.3 — four of the five phantom blockers.

cases.name: one false positive OVER the bound blocks
cases.why: the threshold and the scores disagree, which is a fault in the calibration rather than a weak head. `test_np_threshold.py` already refuses to RETURN such a cut, so seeing one here means something downstream moved it.

cases.name: FALSE NEGATIVES ALONE NEVER BLOCK
cases.why: THE DRIFT ITSELF. NP bounds type-I error and trades recall deliberately; demanding recall 1.000 is a bar nothing learned can clear, and development recall is computed on a corpus particular to one model so its absolute value cannot support a gate. A head that genuinely weakens is caught on held-out acceptance, where two models ARE comparable.

cases.name: many false negatives still do not block on this rule
cases.why: a head that has gone SILENT is a real blocker, but it is a DIFFERENT rule with a different message. Collapsing the two would report one where the other is true.

cases.name: not calibrated to the target rate blocks, whatever the counts
cases.why: too few conformant records to reach the target false-positive rate at all. No threshold can fix that; only more negatives can.

cases.name: no guarantee at all falls back to zero tolerance
cases.why: an uncalibrated head makes no claim about unseen pages, so the only defensible bar is the old one. This is the pre-NP path and must stay strict.

cases.name: no guarantee and no false positives does not block
cases.why: even without a guarantee, false negatives are not a type-I error and are not this rule's business
